27726:
Samuel is the hinge figure between the judges and the kings. Given to God by his mother Hannah and raised at the Shiloh sanctuary, he is called as a boy at a time when the word of the LORD was rare, and grows into a prophet whose words do not fall to the ground. He combines roles no one else in Israel quite holds together: prophet, judge, intercessor and, in practice, priest.

When the elders demand a king like the nations, Samuel resists, warns them of the cost, and then obeys God by anointing Saul. When Saul disobeys, Samuel announces his rejection and secretly anoints David, the youngest son of Jesse. He spends the rest of his life grieving over Saul while shielding David.

Later biblical writers remember him chiefly as a man of prayer: Jeremiah pairs him with Moses as Israel's great intercessors, and the New Testament treats him as the first of the prophets after Moses.
27727: Son of Elkanah and Hannah, dedicated from birth and raised at Shiloh (1 Sam 1-2). Called by God (1 Sam 3), judged Israel all his life on a circuit from Ramah (1 Sam 7:15-17), anointed Saul (1 Sam 10:1) and then David (1 Sam 16:13). 1 Chronicles places him in a Levitical genealogy (1 Chr 6:28) and credits him with records of David's reign (1 Chr 29:29). Acts calls him the start of the prophets (Acts 3:24).
27728: Samuel is ranked alongside Moses and Aaron (Ps 99:6). The Talmud credits him with writing the books of Judges, Ruth and his own book (completed by Gad and Nathan). Some rabbinic readings understand him as a lifelong Nazirite.
27729: Honoured as a prophet and saint (feast 20 August). His call is read as a model of vocation and listening ('Speak, for your servant hears'), and his anointing of David as pointing to Christ the Anointed.
27731: Emphasis falls on Samuel as faithful intercessor and on the theology of the monarchy: the request for a king was sinful in its motive, yet God used kingship for his purposes, leading to David and the messianic line.

27788:
Saul son of Kish, a tall Benjaminite, was Israel's first king. Anointed by Samuel in answer to the people's demand for a king, he began with promise: the Spirit came on him, he rescued Jabesh-gilead from the Ammonites, and he fought the Philistines and other enemies on every side.

His reign then unravels through acts of impatient or partial obedience, above all offering sacrifice without Samuel and sparing Agag and Amalek's livestock. Samuel announces that God has rejected him. The rest of the story traces his decline into fear, jealousy of David, violent suspicion, and finally a desperate visit to a medium before he dies on Mount Gilboa.

Saul is one of Scripture's most tragic figures. The narrative is sympathetic to his torment while holding him responsible, and David's lament over him and Jonathan is among the most moving poems in the Bible.
27789: Son of Kish of Benjamin, taller than anyone (1 Sam 9:2). Anointed by Samuel (1 Sam 10:1), confirmed after victory at Jabesh (1 Sam 11). Rejected for disobedience (1 Sam 13:13-14; 15:23). Tormented by an evil spirit from the LORD (1 Sam 16:14), pursued David, died at Gilboa (1 Sam 31). The length of his reign is textually damaged in 1 Sam 13:1; Acts 13:21 gives forty years. Chronicles says he died for unfaithfulness and for consulting a medium (1 Chr 10:13-14).
27790: Rabbinic tradition is relatively gentle on Saul, noting his humility (hiding among the baggage) and the fact that he sinned fewer times than David; his downfall is attributed to misplaced mercy and failure to obey precisely. Some midrashim stress that he went to his death knowingly, accepting judgment.
27792: Saul often serves as a type of the person who begins in grace but falls through pride and disobedience; Gregory the Great used him as an example for rulers. Debate continues on whether the figure at Endor was truly Samuel or a demonic deception.
27793: Saul illustrates that external anointing and spiritual experience do not equal saving faith; his rejection shows God's sovereignty in choosing David. Some Reformed writers stress his culpability; others note God's providence in giving the people the king they asked for.
27794: Many scholars think the narrative was shaped in David's court to legitimise David's dynasty, so Saul may have been a more effective ruler than portrayed. Others argue the text's own sympathy for Saul tells against crude propaganda.

27799: Partial obedience and blame-shifting regarding Amalek (1 Sam 15)

The Philistines held a monopoly on iron-working (1 Sam 13:19-22) and garrisons in the hill country. Tell el-Ful north of Jerusalem is commonly identified with Gibeah, though excavated remains there are debated.
27807: His failure shapes the Bible's theology of kingship: a king must be subject to God's word through the prophet. His house survived briefly through Ish-bosheth, and his grandson Mephibosheth was cared for by David. The apostle Paul, also a Benjaminite named Saul, was named after him (Acts 13:21; Phil 3:5).

The question is debated.

27909:
David son of Jesse is the central king of the Old Testament: a shepherd boy anointed by Samuel, the giant-killer of the Valley of Elah, a fugitive from Saul who refused to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, and finally the king who united the tribes, captured Jerusalem and made it the political and religious capital of Israel.

God's covenant with him in 2 Samuel 7, promising a house and a throne forever, becomes the foundation of Israel's messianic hope. Prophets look for a coming son of David, and the New Testament opens by calling Jesus the son of David. Many psalms are linked to him by their headings, and he is remembered as Israel's model worshipper.

The text does not idealise him. His adultery with Bathsheba and murder of Uriah are told in plain detail, and the second half of his reign is shadowed by violence within his own family: Amnon's rape of Tamar, Absalom's revolt and death, and the struggle over succession. His greatness in the narrative lies less in moral perfection than in his repentance and his trust in God's mercy.
27910: Youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem (1 Sam 16:10-13). Anointed by Samuel; killed Goliath (1 Sam 17); fled Saul; anointed king at Hebron, ruling seven and a half years there and thirty-three in Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:4-5). Received God's covenant of an everlasting dynasty (2 Sam 7:12-16). Committed adultery and murder, was rebuked by Nathan and repented (2 Sam 11-12). Called a man after God's own heart (1 Sam 13:14; Acts 13:22). Seventy-three psalms carry 'of David' in their Hebrew headings.
27911: David is the ideal king and ancestor of the Messiah (Mashiach ben David). Rabbinic tradition credits him with composing or compiling the book of Psalms and treats his repentance as a model of teshuvah. The Talmud debates the extent of his sin with Bathsheba, some sages arguing soldiers' wives were conditionally divorced, a view others reject.
27912: David is honoured as prophet and saint and as a type of Christ, the shepherd-king born in Bethlehem. Psalm 51 became the church's classic penitential psalm, and the Psalter attributed to him is the backbone of the daily office.
27913: The Davidic covenant is a key stage in covenant theology, fulfilled in Christ, the son of David who reigns forever (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:29-36). David's sin and forgiveness illustrate justification apart from works (Rom 4:6-8).
27914: The Tel Dan inscription (9th century BC) is widely read as mentioning the 'House of David', supporting a historical founder. Scholars debate the size of his kingdom: maximalists accept a substantial state; minimalists and some archaeologists (low chronology) see a modest chiefdom later idealised. Many also read the Succession Narrative (2 Sam 9-20; 1 Kgs 1-2) as either court apologetic or unusually candid royal history.
27916: Refusal to seize the throne by violence against Saul (1 Sam 24:6)
27920: Adultery with Bathsheba and murder of Uriah (2 Sam 11)
27921: Passivity after Amnon raped Tamar (2 Sam 13:21)
27924: Deathbed instructions for revenge on Joab and Shimei (1 Kgs 2:5-9)
27930: David rose in the gap left by declining Egyptian and Hittite power, before Assyria's expansion, when small states could form in the Levant. Philistine pressure, the Saulide-Judahite rivalry and the neutral Jebusite city of Jerusalem explain many of his political moves. Excavations in the City of David (e.g. the Stepped Stone Structure) and at Khirbet Qeiyafa are cited in debates about 10th-century Judah.
27931: Founder of the dynasty that ruled Judah for about four centuries, organiser of Israel's worship (1 Chr 15-16; 23-26), and the figure through whom messianic hope is expressed: Isa 11:1, Jer 23:5, Ezek 34:23-24. Jesus is called son of David (Matt 1:1) and the root and offspring of David (Rev 22:16).
27932: David was the author or editor of the whole book of Psalms, compiling also psalms by ten elders.
27933: A building on Mount Zion has been venerated as David's tomb since the medieval period; most archaeologists consider it unlikely to be authentic, since 1 Kgs 2:10 places the tomb in the City of David.
27935: Islam honours David (Dawud) as a prophet to whom the Zabur (Psalms) was given.
27937: Passionate and poetic; moves quickly from boldness to tears, speaks to God as to a close friend, and turns crises into songs.

Her quick action and wise speech kept David from avenging himself on Nabal, and her words anticipated God's 'sure house' for David. After Nabal's death she became David's wife, shared his outlaw years at Ziklag, and bore him a son at Hebron.

27958: Calm, gracious and persuasive; uses careful courtesy and theological argument to turn an angry man aside.
